title: Job 7:8–14
context: The speaker is Job, now addressing God. He pictures his death: those who see him will see him no more, and God’s eyes will look for him, but he will not be there. Like a cloud that vanishes, one who goes down to Sheol, the place of the dead, does not come up again or return to his house. Therefore Job refuses to keep silent and voices his complaint in bitterness of soul. He asks whether he is a sea or a sea monster that God should set a guard over him, and says that even his bed gives no relief, for God frightens him with dreams and visions. His view of death reflects his own limited horizon in the midst of suffering.

verses.text: The eye of him who sees me will see me no more. Your eyes will be on me, but I will not be.
verses.arminianNotes: Job says those who see him will see him no more, and God’s eyes will seek him but he will be gone. Arminian readers see Job imagining his death and the end of all relationship, even with God.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the poignancy of Job picturing God looking for him too late. Both traditions read the verse as an expression of Job’s despair, shaped by his limited view of what lies beyond death.

verses.text: As the cloud is consumed and vanishes away, so he who goes down to Sheol will come up no more.
verses.arminianNotes: Like a vanishing cloud, one who goes down to Sheol does not come up again. Arminian readers read the verse within Job’s limited horizon, describing death as he sees it in his anguish.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Sheol is the place of the dead, and they read Job’s words in light of later revelation about resurrection. Shared ground: both traditions hedge the verse as Job’s view in suffering, not a full teaching on the afterlife.

verses.text: He will return no more to his house, neither will his place know him any more.
verses.arminianNotes: The dead man returns no more to his house, and his place knows him no more. Arminian readers note the finality Job feels, as he pictures his household going on without him.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the language as a poetic picture of human mortality, compare Psalm 103:16 by reference. Both traditions read the verse as completing Job’s reflection on death’s apparent finality.

verses.text: “Therefore I will not keep silent. I will speak in the anguish of my spirit. I will complain in the bitterness of my soul.
verses.arminianNotes: Job declares he will not keep silent but will speak in anguish and complain in bitterness. Arminian readers see the honesty of lament as permitted within faith, as Job brings his complaint to God.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see in Job’s resolve a model of bringing even bitter words to God rather than turning away from him. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as affirming that lament has a place in the life of faith.

verses.text: Am I a sea, or a sea monster, that you put a guard over me?
verses.arminianNotes: Job asks if he is a sea or a sea monster that God must guard him. Arminian readers note that some see an allusion to ancient pictures of the sea as a chaotic power, though such analogies are hedged.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that elsewhere God sets limits on the sea (compare Job 38:8–11), which may lie behind Job’s image. Both traditions read Job’s question as feeling himself treated as a threat to be restrained.

verses.text: When I say, ‘My bed will comfort me. My couch will ease my complaint,’
verses.arminianNotes: Job hopes his bed will comfort him and his couch ease his complaint. Arminian readers note the simple longing for rest, which suffering denies him even in sleep.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the verse as setting up the contrast with the dreams that follow. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as Job’s honest description of seeking relief and finding none.

verses.text: then you scare me with dreams and terrify me through visions,
verses.arminianNotes: Job says God frightens him with dreams and terrifies him with visions. Arminian readers note that Job attributes his torment directly to God, speaking as he feels in his anguish.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Job does not know of the heavenly scene in chapters 1–2, and speaks from within his suffering. Both traditions read the verse as Job’s perception, not as the book’s settled verdict on God’s character.
